He became one the foremost of the followers of the Bab. Subsequently losing all his family properties, cast in the deep dungeon jail for four months where he became aware of his destiny, later writing. “When I contemplate, O my God, the relationship the bindeth me to Thee, I am moved to proclaim to all created things “verily I am God”; and when I consider my own self, lo, find it courser than clay."  Then he and many Babis were banished to Bagdad arriving April 8,1953. Before his passing the evening of May 29, 1892, Baha’u’llah had written over 15,000 tablets and epistles. His Will designated his oldest son Abdu'l Baha, (Servant of God) 1850-1922, born the evening of the Babs declaration, his sole successor and Head of The Baha’i Faith.

And while we generally accept that this is the way the internet works these days, you have to admit - such a brazen reminder we’re being watched is a bit creepy. More unsettling still is when you’ve only mentioned that product in face-to-face conversation. How does the internet know about that? Looking for the simplest explanation, &nbsp; it’s hard to ignore the microphone you’re carrying around in your pocket, and you don’t have to be wearing a tin-foil hat to start drawing some fairly alarming conclusions. But before we go too far down that rabbit-hole, I should say that while I definitely understand the logic of that thought process, personally I’m pretty confident your phone isn’t listening to your conversations in order to advertise to you. Primarily because the risks far outweigh anything that companies would stand to gain. I’m not saying that they wouldn’t gain anything from listening in - I’m just saying they don’t have to. Because when it comes to targeting you with weirdly specific adverts, they’ve already got all the information they need. Let me explain. Advertising is all about demographics - dividing people up into categories. The more information a company has about you, the more specific they can make the adverts you see. As an example of just how far this can go, let’s look at what we share with Facebook, one of the more notable offenders. First there’s the basics - age, job, relationship status. Already these put you in some demographic boxes. But you also post on Facebook about your hobbies - ones you do regularly, ones you’ve tried, or even just want to try. Maybe you join groups for TV shows or films you like, or follow your favourite authors, actors, content creators. All of this data can be - and is - harvested, and all of it represents advertising demographics that Facebook is putting you in. But it doesn’t end there. You might check in to places you go - favourite restaurants, your gym. Or tourist attractions, in which case Facebook knows you’re travelling. And even if you don’t check in, if the app has access to Location Services, it knows where you are most of the time anyway. Forget about Facebook knowing where you shop online - it knows where you shop in real life. You freely shared all of this information with Facebook, and its terms of service let it use that data however it wants - which includes trading it with other companies. But where do the face-to-face conversations come in? Well, Facebook doesn’t only have this information on you - they also have it on your friends, as well as knowing how much you speak to and see those friends. Combining all of this data adds a whole new dimension. Meet three friends - Alice, Bob and Charlie. Alice buys Product X online. A week later, Alice goes to see Bob. Three days after that, Bob buys Product X. And when, a few days later, Alice goes to see Charlie, Facebook’s algorithm starts to do its thing. Based on knowing about the three friends’ shared interests, Alice’s purchase, Alice and Bob’s interaction, and Bob’s subsequent purchase, Facebook deduces that a) Alice probably told Bob about Product X, b) She might have also told Charlie about Product X, and c) Even if she didn’t, Charlie might be interested anyway. Soon after, Charlie starts seeing adverts for Product X. Now, if Alice didn’t tell Charlie, Charlie has no reason to think this advert is strange. But if Alice did tell Charlie, then both Alice and Charlie now think these adverts are direct evidence that their phones are listening to them, even though the reality is far more complicated, and in my opinion, far more alarming. Because my point here isn’t “our phones aren’t listening to us so we should all stop worrying”, it’s sort of the opposite. We should be more concerned that we’ve freely volunteered enough data about our tastes, movements, and interactions that we’ve made tapping our phones entirely unnecessary. The bottom line is that however that data was obtained, if it can be triangulated to make accurate predictions about our shopping preferences, the thought of what else it could do should be enough to give us pause. So if you think you’re sharing too much personal information, or you don’t trust the services you’re using, you can, and should, take control of your own data, and vote with your feet. Because most of the time on the internet, if you’re not paying for the product, you are the product.

- Facebook Advertising Costs In 2026 | How Much Should You Spend in Facebook Ads?: Kind: captions Language: en How much do Facebook ads cost? It's the number one question I hear every single week. And honestly, it's a fair one because I've seen businesses spend $1,400 on ads and generate $391,000 in revenue. But I've also seen businesses spend the same exact amount and barely break even. So, the real question is not how much do Facebook ads cost, it's how much should you spend to actually get results. That's what I'm breaking down for you today. And in case you don't know, I'm Brandy with Life Marketing, the digital marketing agency with a mission to help small businesses grow. Otherwise, for everybody else looking to figure out Facebook ads themselves, I'm going to walk you through exactly how Facebook ad costs work in 2026, what factors actually drive those costs, and how to set the right budget for your business without overspending. So, the first thing we need to talk about is how Facebook ad costs actually work. Facebook does not charge you for sales. And unlike Google ads, it also doesn't charge you per click. It charges you for impressions or the number of times your ad is seen. And this is important to clarify right out of the gates because impressions are different than reach. Reach is the number of unique individuals who saw your ad. And impressions is the amount of times your ad was seen. So, if your reach is 10,000, that means 10,000 different people saw your ad. If you got 10,000 impressions, that technically could mean the same person saw your ad 10,000 times. So, you'll want to look at both your reach and your impressions in your ads manager later when you're looking at how your ads are performing. But, it's important to understand the difference now because Facebook measures something called CPM, which stands for cost per thousand impressions. So, for example sake, let's assume your impressions are the same as your reach in this example. If your CPM is $10, then $100 will get your ad in front of about 10,000 people. Whereas, if your CPM is $20, that same $100 will only reach 5,000 people. That's why two businesses with the same budget can see totally different outcomes because your money buys eyeballs, not results. So, now let's talk about what can cause that and why Facebook CPMs vary. Why do some businesses pay $10 CPM? while others pay 20 or more. There are three big reasons. Number one is ad relevance. Facebook rewards ads that people engage with. Engagement being a click, watch, share, or conversion. Highquality ads equal lower cost, and crappy ads equal higher cost. Think of it as Facebook saying, "If people like your ads, we will show them for cheaper." Number two is audience size. Bigger audience equals cheaper cost. niche tiny audiences equals more expensive because more advertisers are fighting for fewer eyeballs. So, for example, targeting all parents in the US will almost always cost less per impression than moms of newborn twins in one zip code. And a pro tip I'll throw in here is that the Facebook algorithm has evolved so much over the last few years, it can read your ad copy and image and URL on its own and make a decision of who to show your ad to based on those things. you're actually constricting its ability to do that if you get too narrowed down in the targeting. So, not only is broader targeting better for your wallet, it's also usually better for your results. And number three, competition. The more advertisers chasing the same group, the more expensive it gets. For example, a lot of businesses like to target people by their birthday month and offer them a free birthday gift as a sort of lead magnet to capture email addresses. The problem with that is that everybody has that idea. So targeting by birthday months is usually a highly competitive and therefore highly expensive [music] Facebook ad strategy. So your costs are not random. They're shaped by your relevance, your reach, and your rivals. Now that we understand that, let's answer the magic question. What should your Facebook ad budget actually be? The truth is it depends on your stage of business and your goals. So let's look at a couple examples. If nobody knows you exist, you're in the awareness stage. You'll need to spend more upfront to introduce yourself to the market. Think of it like planting seeds. You're paying to build an audience that you can retarget later. I would plan on spending $2 to $3,000 minimum just to build awareness and a retargeting pool. If you already have website visitors or followers coming in from somewhere, you're already in the retargeting stage. And retargeting ads are cheaper and convert better because those ads are being delivered to people who already know you and are familiar with your brand. You can usually start seeing sales traction with $500 to $1,000 a month focused on retargeting. If you're selling higher ticket offers like a thousand or more, expect a longer sales cycle and higher spend. On average, people need seven touch points with a brand before they have enough trust built to buy from that brand. And that number usually increases the more expensive the product or service is. So, don't expect to spend $500 and make 25 sales. That's unrealistic. A better goal would be to break even early and then scale once you have proof your ads work. And lastly, number four, if you're cash strapped, please do not put your last dollar into Facebook ads. Ads are an investment, and you need the room to test, tweak, and sometimes lose money before you gain money. Only spend what you can comfortably risk. Ads are like fuel in a tank. The more you put in, the further you can go, but only if your car is running right. And on that note, let's now talk about why your media matters. What kind of content are you running? The answer to that question could determine if your Facebook ad costs are higher or lower. Video ads, for example, almost always perform better. They get cheaper CPMs, higher engagement, and more conversions. Static images can work, but they usually cost more per result. Unless, for instance, you're in a specific niche like photography, where people are wanting to see static images as a testament to your work. If you can test video, simple, authentic videos from your phone can beat polished graphics because they feel more real. On social media, people don't want a commercial. They don't want something that feels like an ad or disrupts their scrolling. So, the more authentic and casual and organic the video feels, the better. And the last thing I'll say about the contents of your ad is that I hope they are customer focused and not business focused. A lot of times, small business owners are so proud of what they've built. They spend their whole ad talking about their business, their team, what they've accomplished, their product features, their service features, the awards they've won, and so on. But customers don't care about any of that. The bottom line is that they care about how they benefit from giving you their attention and ultimately their money. You have to earn both with value focused content. Solve pain points for your customers that they struggle with. Provide value that will help them achieve their goals. That's what the content of your ad should be about. Now, let's talk about the timeline that actually works. The biggest mistake we see businesses make is that they blow their entire budget in one month and then quit. Facebook ads do not work that way. It takes 6 months minimum to properly test, optimize, and [music] scale. Because remember, you're not just running ads. You're testing audiences, testing creatives, testing offers, testing landing pages, and building retargeting pools. So instead of dumping $5,000 into one month, stretch that over 6 months. That's about $850 a month. If you can stretch to $7,000, that's about $1,200 a month. [music] Enough to start layering in advanced features like retargeting and lookalike audiences. Think marathon, not sprinting. Facebook ads pay off for businesses that stick with the process. And lastly, I want to leave you with hidden costs to look for that aren't really hidden. Technically, Facebook does not add extra fees, but here are things you may need to invest in to get the most out of your ads. A solid website or landing page because traffic without conversions is wasted money. Just the other day in our chat, one of our clients had a huge breakthrough in sales after switching their checkout process to Shopify. strong creative videos, images, copywriting, and if you're short on time, hiring an agency or ad manager to run it right. These aren't mandatory, but they can make the difference between ads that flop, and ads that fuel your business and make your investment worth it. So, in short, Facebook ads cost whatever you budget. But CPMs are shaped by relevance, audience size, and competition. Your budget should depend on where your business is at, awareness, retargeting, or scaling. video usually wins. And if you're serious, commit to at least 6 months of consistent spend. General rule, budget $5,000 to $7,000 over 6 months to properly test if Facebook ads will work for your business. - How to Fix Event Duplication Issues in Facebook Ads (2026 Guide): Kind: captions Language: en In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to fix event duplication issues in Facebook ads. Event duplication happens when the same action, like a purchase, lead, or add to cart gets recorded more than once that inflates your numbers, confuses optimization, and can waste budget. We'll walk through a clear process to diagnose and fix it so your reporting is accurate, and your campaigns can actually learn. Start by understanding why duplication occurs. The most common cause is when the Facebook pixel and the conversions API both send the same event without proper duplication. It can also happen if multiple pixels are installed on your site, if an event fires twice on page load, or if browser and server version of the same event don't share a matching event ID. Next, open Facebook Events Manager. Select your pixel and head to diagnostics. This is where Facebook surfaces warnings about duplicate events. If you see messages about purchase or lead events being sent twice, you're on the right track. From there, identify exactly where duplicates are coming from. Typical culprits include a pixel installed both in your website's code and in Google Tag Manager. a platform integration like Shopify or WooCommerce combined with a manual pixel or an event that fires on a button click and again on the thank you page. Trace each event's origin so you know what to keep and what to disable. Dduplication depends on using the same event ID for both the pixel and the conversions API version of an event. For example, a purchase event might use an order number as the event power ID, such as order 1 2 3 4 5. The key is consistency. The browser event and the server event must share the exact same ID so Facebook can count it once. Then remove extra pixel installations. Check your site source code. Review Google Tag Manager and inspect your CMS or ecommerce settings. Keep a single pixel firing per event and avoid overlapping configurations. Use the test events tool in events manager to validate your fixes. Perform real actions on your site and watch the stream. Each event should appear only once. If you still see duplicates, revisit your triggers and integrations. Address platform specifics carefully. On Shopify, stick to the native Facebook integration. On Woo Commerce, turn off any manual pixel if a plug-in is active. In Google Tag Manager, audit triggers to prevent the same event from firing twice. Don't delete events at random. Always identify the source before removing anything. You'll know it's fixed when diagnostics shows no duplication warnings. Test events shows a single fire per action and your conversion numbers look realistic. Follow this workflow to improve tracking accuracy, help Facebook optimize better, and prevent wasted ad spend.

It might look like messages, profile visits, engagement. These are signals that your message is working. Reason number seven, you don't review your ads properly. You see, when ads don't work, most people panic instead of reviewing what went on with the ad. You should be checking. Are people watching my video? Are they clicking? Are they engaging? This will tell you what to fix, not whether to quit. So what do you do instead? Now whether you sell product or services, here is what actually works for you. Number one, speak to the problem first. Number 3: Focus your ads, target long-tail keywords rather than shorter broad terms Having a bigger account with a bigger budget typically means a lot more work and time is needed to optimise everything. The big dogs are likely to have a team looking over huge accounts with tons of keywords, running multiple ads directing to who knows how many landing pages. As a smaller business, with less budget, you can take the time to target specific keywords and key terms that your bigger competitors might miss because it’s not as obvious or is a little too niche. In fact, there’s even value in targeting low volume keywords which we’ve covered in a previous episode of Giant Wednesday and that might be something that gives you an advantage over competitors. Number 4: bid on high-volume keywords, but it’s all about the timing This doesn’t mean that you shouldn’t be bidding on high-volume keywords. In fact, high volume keywords can help you build out those super targeted and specific campaigns of yours they expose those high converting keywords that your competitors might be missing. But, we all know how quickly that budget can be spent if you’re not hot on it. Which is why you need to be strict on when and how long you bid for. Spend some time analysing the data of your ads account. What time of the day do you see the most success? What are the most engaging days of the week? Google ads has some super clever targeting settings which allows you to adjust bids and ads being served based on different days of the week and even time of day, you’ll get that all-important exposure by just being more clever about how and when your ads serve without running your budget dry. It’s super important to keep your account tidy, so do those checks and negative out irrelevant terms. Number 5: Don’t forget about your landing pages It can be so easy to get caught up in getting those clicks and competing against the big boys that you forget about what happens once you DO get in front of the right people. The user’s journey once they arrive at your site is so important! After all, just because they’ve clicked, doesn’t mean it's a sure thing that they’re going to convert... By having the freedom of choosing the landing page especially for your PPC audience, you have the ability to send users to your highest converting landing pages, encouraging them over the conversion finishing line. Having this freedom also allows you to create specific PPC landing pages, if you want, to include some great unique selling points for your business, it gives you the ability to show off a bit, add reviews, testimonials and other engaging content to show the user that you really are the right fit for them. which means more budget to spend across other keywords! Your landing pages don’t have to be perfect from the get-go. You can experiment with them and run A/B split testing This will give you the ability to see which page works best, and adjust your campaigns accordingly In fact, I’ll link in the YouTube description below to an episode on making unbelievable landing pages AND split testing so you can keep on learning today, lucky you! And there you have it, five pieces of advice from me to you on how to match up (if not better) than your competitors that may have a larger PPC budget than you. Remember - it’s not always about how much budget you have to spend, it’s about how you spend it that matters. hopefully you’re now ready to go optimise everything you’ve been doing and adapt your PPC strategy to compete successfully. ! In any case, we've seen large language models in particular grow 2,000 times in size over the last five years. And of course, their environmental costs are rising as well. The most recent work I led, found that switching out a smaller, more efficient model for a larger language model emits 14 times more carbon for the same task. Like telling that knock-knock joke. I helped create CodeCarbon, a tool that runs in parallel to AI training code that estimates the amount of energy it consumes and the amount of carbon it emits. But, two things we do need to talk about are the buying types and the campaign objective. So, we've got two different buying types. We've got auction, and we've got reservation. Auction is just the cost of your Facebook and Instagram ads is going to be determined by simple market forces, demand and supply. More demand, higher cost. Less demand, lower cost. And that's demand from advertisers, by the way. How many advertisers there are, how much they're willing to spend. Uh reservation, you can actually guarantee a certain price, often a lower price. And and the cost of Facebook and Instagram advertising is normally measured in CPMs. So, cost per 1,000 impressions. So, it's cheaper to use reservation, but that's not the option I'd recommend you use, which might sound bizarre. Here's why. In order for Meta to be able to guarantee that lower cost, they are going to put your ads in front of lower quality prospects, or lower quality ad placements. The better quality ad impressions are usually seen through auction, and that's a big deal. So, I'd recommend you go with auction. Let's move on to campaign objective. So, you've got six different options here, and they do different things. And your campaign objective is really, really important because it's going to inform how Meta optimizes your campaign. So, you're basically saying to Meta, "This is what I want." And Meta's really powerful machine learning and AI-based systems are going to optimize your ads, work out who to advertise to, what time of day, how often, all those things to get you more of what you want. That's why it's so important to get your campaign objective set up correctly. So, you've got awareness. Awareness is where Meta will put your ads in front of people that are most likely to remember them. Put your ads in front of as many people as possible. Not an option I typically recommend for beginners or for businesses operating with a relatively small Facebook and Instagram ad budget because it can be quite an easy way in those scenarios to spend a bunch of money and not really see anything back for it. What we see with awareness is it can work really well for larger businesses with big budgets because awareness takes time and it takes a lot of ad impressions across a lot of people over an extended period. Bigger businesses have those budgets, smaller ones and beginners to to Meta ads typically don't. This is a shift that has happened. The old algorithm is now the new Andromeda algorithm. What we need to understand here is what is this shift? Why is it so important? And how are we adapting to it with structure first. So, first off, the Andromeda algorithm has been a shift from audience to creative targeting. Now, what this very simply means is in the old algorithm, you would choose your audience, whether it's broad, interest, lookalikes, whatever, and the creatives you push into that ad set get targeted from that interest group. This has now flipped. Instead of an interest or a broad target deciding who the ads are going to be shown to, that has completely reversed. We now have a situation where whatever ads are within your ad set define the targeting on an individual level. This means that, yes, you could have completely different ads in the same ad set that target two very different people. It also means that you could have multiple ad sets in the same campaign targeting completely different people, even if the targeting, the interest group, or the broad is 100% the same. Now, I don't want to get too conceptual on this, but what this means is that your creative concepts matter more than ever. And the structure that we actually like to deploy to solve for Andromeda that we've proven out across 80-plus accounts at this point is one of with swim lanes. Now, swim lanes are a very simple philosophy that we need to separate prospecting, retargeting, and retention. So, the important part about swim lanes is that you as the advertiser actually know where you're spending your money. One of the biggest flaws that we see with Facebook is that it overspends on engage and existing customers. It's fine to spend a lot of money on engage. It's fine to spend a lot of money on existing customers. But what I don't like is when advertisers or brands that we work with think that they're spending money on prospects. They think they're spending money on new customers when in reality, they're actually spending a boatload of that cash on existing and engage, which they believe they're targeting in other places like email, SMS, and other retargeting methods. What we like to do is make sure that our swim lanes are clearly defined. Our first swim lane is prospecting. This is generally a CBO prospecting campaign mixed with a boatload of ad sets. Those could be a combination of broad and interest groups, even lookalikes if you'd like to give them a shot. The important part is that we're grouping a lot together in one campaign, and we are creating a hyper-competitive environment. I want to actually say that twice. A hyper-competitive environment is one of the most important things that you could have in a Facebook ads account because you're actually giving the algorithm some power to decide where to spend your money. Now, this is very, very different than a one campaign method or just throwing everything into one ad set because you could actually define minimum, maximum budgets and even put exclusions on things at the ad set level within your prospecting campaigns. That's the control, that's the levers that we like to have on our side without just giving all the power to Facebook. The second and third swim lanes are retargeting and retention. Retargeting is anyone who's visited your site and anyone who's engaged with your business. They know about you, very simple. Retention, on the other hand, is anyone who's purchased. This isn't someone who's added to cart. This isn't someone who almost purchased. They've handed you money. That is a very big difference between retargeting and retention. We want to make sure we're treating each of these buckets separately, we're dedicating our budget accordingly, and even in some cases curating the creative to each of these buckets. But most of the time, it's okay to have the same creatives in each with a big testing environment in our prospecting CBO. And you might ask, why? Why does this fix Andromeda? Why does this fix the issue that everyone seems to have in the back of their mind? It's actually quite simple. It starts in the prospecting CBO campaign. The prospecting CBO campaign now has the capability to spend its cash wherever it wants, meaning your audiences can individually be targeted per creative. So, think about it like this. If you separated all of your ad sets or all of your creative concepts into different campaigns, then you're controlling the budget. $200 here, $200 here, $200 here. But grouping these together, what it actually does is it allows you to still see very clearly with organized ad sets, set minimums and maximum budgets if you need, and with your total budget, so 200, 200, 200 equaling 600 on a total CBO budget, Facebook will distribute wherever the cash is best spent. And I know one issue that a lot of people have is that certain creatives don't get any spend. I'm here to tell you this is a feature, not a bug, most of the time. Not all the time. Most of the time, Facebook is saving you cash by doing this. So, what I would advise, if you really feel like there's an ad that you've put a lot of time or effort into, set a minimum budget, make sure it gets $25, $50 a day, let it ramp up a little bit. If it doesn't work after 7 days, kill that minimum budget. Okay, so our structures are complete. The second shift that I have seen and that basically everyone has seen because it actually happened. But now, targeting and really all the features are kind of coming back to us, which is a good thing. it comes to measurement, this is one of the places where we need to be accurate. Now, I want to challenge all of these third-party attribution softwares because they do have their place, but I think people get too excited about them when we actually have the best tool natively built into Facebook. Think about it like this. Hyros, Triple Whale, and all third-party attribution platforms have only access to certain amounts of data. Imagine Facebook only had click-based data. The only signal that we were able to optimize on and the only algorithm input was click-based purchases. And that is exactly what Meta is capable of doing with its standard attribution. It sounds so boring because it's built in, and there's fancy tools with great marketing slogans that actually sell us into programs that don't do as much as the actual Facebook tracking. And I don't want to discredit these tools because there are some use cases where they're great. But when it comes to measurement, the best measurement is Meta's measurement. They care so much about it. I was at a Facebook conference just a few months ago where they were breaking down their improvements to the measurement.
